messages.content: Explain why the Moon appears to change shape during a month.

response: The Moon appears to change shape throughout the month because Earth observers see different amounts of the Moon's sunlit surface as it orbits the Earth. A full Moon occurs when the Moon is on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun, so the Sun illuminates the side of the Moon that faces away from Earth. As the Moon moves in its orbit, the fraction of the Moon's disk that appears illuminated appears to grow (wax) and then shrink (wane) — this is the Moon's phase cycle. The Moon completes this cycle in about 29.5 days, which is why we have approximately two complete phases (full to full or new to new) each month. The apparent size of the Moon also appears to change slightly throughout the month — this is called lunar libration and is caused by the Moon's elliptical orbit and its axial tilt, not to be confused with the phase cycle.

Multiply or divide the numerator and denominator of each fraction by the same number so they share a denominator. messages.content: Explain why a metal spoon can feel colder than a wooden one in the same room.

response: A metal spoon will feel colder to the touch than a wooden one, even if they have been sitting in the same room for the same amount of time. This is because metal is a better conductor of heat than wood. The temperature of a material is a measure of the average kinetic energy of its molecules — warmer molecules move faster and cooler ones move slower. In the air, molecules are constantly colliding and moving around. When you place a metal object in a room, the slightly faster-moving air molecules hit the metal and transfer some of their energy to the metal molecules, causing them to vibrate more and the metal to appear warmer to the touch. Because wood is a poorer conductor, the air molecules hit the wood and get reflected back with less of their energy transferred, so the wood remains closer to the air temperature. Your hand, being warmer than the air, transfers more energy to the metal in a shorter time than to the wood, making the metal feel colder. This is why a metal spoon handles are often much colder than the wood handle of a knife after it has been in a cold freezer — the metal has simply done a better job of sharing its heat with the surroundings.
